the diff shows only this PR's three commits). DeepSeek-V4.1's layers past the last KV-source layer (21-39 on V4.1-Flash) own nothing but sliding-window KV: every later layer attends the compressed KV of the source layers, and only the last 128 tokens' window KV is read after prefill. This is DeepSeek's decoder-side SWA bounded replay: in prefill those layers run on each request's last 128 tokens only, cold prefills included, while layers 0-20 still run on every token. It is a deliberate approximation, not an equivalent reduction of work: the kept rows' window attention in layers 21-39 is bounded at the trailing window (the SWA kernels read no window KV below it), so the last token's hidden state is not bit-identical to a full prefill; the long-range context reaches it through the compressed KV. The accuracy runs below (gsm8k on TP4 and DP4, two passes each) and DSpark's unchanged acceptance length are what this rests on.\nDeepseekV4Model\n(\nnvidia/model.py\n): when the layers after the last KV source are all sliding-window and the configuration allows it, the forward is split into\n_run_layers\nup to the cut,\nDecoderReplayLayers\nfor the rest, and the final mHC collapse. Everything lives in persistent buffers because that graph reads them by address. The result is set on\nDecoderReplayLayers.replay_batch\n; it is None when nothing trims in an eager forward and under FULL graphs (uniform decode).\nDecoderReplayLayers\n(\ndecoder_replay_layers.py\n): gathers the seven layer inputs by the rows, runs the layers under a copy of the forward context with the replay batch's attention metadata, slot mappings, padding mask, batch descriptor and DP metadata, and scatters the outputs back to full-batch rows. Under breakable piecewise graphs the replay is an eager break of the model graph: the layers run in a graph of their own (\nReplayCudaGraphs\n, keyed by the replay batch's padded size) captured inside the model graph's capture of the same size. Only prefills trim, so a capture's dummy batch keeps all its rows and every capture size gets a replay graph of that size; at runtime the replay batch pads to the smallest capture size that fits, which therefore always exists.\nData parallelism: the replay layers' MoE collectives need every rank's token count, so the model state has the ranks agree in\nprepare_attn\nwith one CPU all-reduce carrying whether each rank trims and its replay token count. Recursive doubling within power-of-two blocks, then one concurrent exchange\n+    between blocks. Results are bitwise identical across ranks. Works with\n+    stateless (unregistered) process groups.\n+    \"\"\"\n+    world_size = group.size()\n+    if world_size == 1:\n+        return tensor\n+    block_size = world_size & -world_size\n+    num_blocks = world_size // block_size\n+    if tensor.device.type != \"cpu\" or not tensor.is_contiguous():\n+        torch.distributed.all_reduce(tensor, group=group)\n+        return tensor\n+\n+    rank = group.rank()\n+    tag = _CPU_ALL_REDUCE_TAG_BASE\n+\n+    # Recursive doubling within the block (peers stay in the aligned block).\n+    if block_size > 1:\n+        # This branch applies only to even world sizes.\n+        scratch = torch.empty_like(tensor)\n+        mask = 1\n+        while mask < block_size:\n+            peer = rank ^ mask\n+            # Wait for both ops before touching either buffer.\n+            recv_work = group.recv([scratch], peer, tag)\n+            send_work = group.send([tensor], peer, tag)\n+            recv_work.wait()\n+            send_work.wait()\n+            tensor.add_(scratch)\n+            mask <<= 1\n+            tag += 1\n+\n+    # Cache-blind balancing disperses that reuse; fixed affinity preserves it but can overload a server. CacheRoute resolves this tradeoff with a periodic routing plan. It admits high-rate keys to a stable warm set and places their assignments by expected load. Hot keys may use more than one destination, although every key in our primary semi-synthetic \n[... excerpt gap ...]\n\n8 Conclusion\n\n\n\n\nCacheRoute plans prefix affinity and expected load once per control interval. On a 70B fp8 model across 60 H100 GPUs, it reaches 93.2% served KV hit and 2.3\u00d72.3\\times the capacity of the strongest baseline at a 3.5-s p99 SLO. The negative workloads set an equally important boundary: affinity can reduce capacity when the recoverable prefix work is small. Any real deployment would therefore measure its own boundary with shadow replay.\n\n\n\n\n\n\nSupplementary Material\n\n\n\n\nThe supplement records experiment provenance, secondary runs, and negative results. Today, we are excited to introduce\nDeepEP V2\n, which includes a complete refactoring of Expert Parallelism \u2014 achieving extreme performance with several times fewer SM resources compared to V1, while supporting significantly larger scale-up and scale-out domains \u2014 as well as experimental 0 SM Engram, 0 SM Pipeline Parallelism, and 0 SM Context Parallelism all-gather.\nWe are also happy to announce that we have switched from the NVSHMEM backend to the more lightweight\nNCCL Gin backend\n.\nNew Features\nFully JIT (Just-In-Time compilation)\nNCCL Gin backend\nHeader-only & lightweight\nAble to reuse existing NCCL communicators\nEPv2\nCUDA graph compatible, or faster CPU sync in saving memory mode\nHigh-throughput and low-latency APIs unified into a single interface, with a new GEMM layout\nLarger scale-up & scale-out domain support (up to EP2048)\nAnalytical SM & QP count calculation \u2014 no more auto-tuning needed\nBoth hybrid & direct modes remain supported\nFor V3-like legacy training, SM usage reduced from 24 to 4 - 6 while maintaining equivalent or better performance\n0 SM Engram (with RDMA)\n0 SM PP (with RDMA)\n0 SM CP (with Copy Engine)\nNotes\nBuffer size consumption is larger than V1\n0 SM RDMA low-latency EP is no longer supported\nEngram, PP, and CP are experimental features\nStill On-going Features\nElastic GPU & CPU buffers\n: A contiguous virtual address space that maps to a hybrid of GPU and CPU physical memory under the hood, enabling fully automatic and transparent Engram or imbalanced EP\nReducing intermediate buffer sizes by leveraging EP replay to handle load imbalance\nAll-gather updates and reduce-scatter implementations for DP & TP\nPerformance\nFollowing V3's configuration, we tested with 8K tokens per batch, 7168 hidden dimensions, top 8 experts, FP8 dispatching, and BF16 combining, and obtained the following results:\nArch\nNIC type\nTopo\nDispatch Bottleneck Bandwidth\nCombine Bottleneck Bandwidth\n#SMs\nSM90\nCX7\nEP 8 x 2\n90 GB/s (RDMA)\n81 GB/s (RDMA)\n12\nSM90\nCX7\nEP 8 x 4\n61 GB/s (RDMA)\n61 GB/s (RDMA)\n6\nSM100\nCX7\nEP 8 x 2\n90 GB/s (RDMA)\n91 GB/s (RDMA)\n12\nSM100\nN/A\nEP 8\n726 GB/s (NVLink)\n740 GB/s (NVLink)\n64 (Max perf)\nSM100\nN/A\nEP 8\n643 GB/s (NVLink)\n675 GB/s (NVLink)\n24 (Min #SM)\nNotes, the results are logical bandwidth. When a store tile extends past an expert's capacity, it can overwrite valid rows of the next expert. This affects both BF16 and FP8: capacity 32 reproduces it, and capacity 96 also fails when experts are nearly full.\n\nKeep the expert dimension in the output descriptor and reuse the existing 3D TMA store path. This preserves tile selection and the compute pipeline without adding buffers or synchronization. Boundary regressions are integrated into the existing BF16 and FP8 test suites.\n\nThis revisits the limitation discussed in #15 and the small-capacity failure reported in #268. #15 previously fixed small capacities by shrinking the store tile and rejected larger capacities not divisible by the tile size; it also suggested 3D TMA but deferred support for those cases. This change handles both small and non-tile-aligned capacities through the same output path.\n\nOn H200, the median paired latency changes across six rounds were between \u22120.17% and +0.16% for the larger tested shapes. The smallest shape was about 1.9% slower for BF16 and 1.5% slower for FP8, roughly 0.06\u20130.08 \u00b5s. The uniform 3D path avoids maintaining separate aligned and unaligned implementations, at that small measured cost.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Reproduction and validation</summary>\n\nRequires an SM90 GPU and a source build of DeepGEMM. "[Bug] non-deterministic results in sm90 tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm\n#449\nNew issue\nCopy link\nNew issue\nCopy link\nOpen\nOpen\n[Bug] non-deterministic results in sm90 tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm\n#449\nCopy link\nDescription\nleevan\nopened\non Sep 16, 2026\nIssue body actions\nDescription\nOn SM90 GPUs, tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm can produce incorrect and non-deterministic GEMM outputs when processing multiple K blocks.\nRepeated calls with identical inputs can return different results.\nRoot cause\nThe kernel uses asynchronous WGMMA instructions with register-source A operands. Previously, the next iteration loaded its A fragment\nbefore waiting for the preceding iteration's WGMMA to complete. This could overwrite A registers while they were still being read by\nthe in-flight WGMMA.\nFix\nProposed fix:\n#448\nThe fix moves\nwarpgroup_wait<0>()\nimmediately after\nwarpgroup_commit_batch()\n, ensuring that each iteration's WGMMA completes\nbefore its A registers are reused.\nThe PR also adds a regression test covering split-K, PDL enabled/disabled, and default/side streams. It checks outputs against FP32\nreferences and verifies repeatability across identical launches.\nValidation\nWith the fix applied, both the existing hyperconnection tests and all 24 configurations of the new regression test passed on an SM90\nGPU.\nTODO\nfix will introduce some performance regression which suppose to be mitigated in upcoming PRs\u3002\nReactions are currently unavailable\nActivity\nLiRunGuo\ncommented\non\nSep 22, 2026\nLiRunGuo\non Sep 22, 2026\nMore actions\nI measured this on an H200 (SM90, driver 580.159.03, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130) with DeepGEMM\nmain\n(\n78b6900\n), in case it helps the review of\n#448\n.\nReproduction.\nI ran the 24 shapes from\ntest_hc_prenorm_gemm\n(\nm\nin 13 / 137 / 4096 / 8192,\nn = 24\n,\nk\nin 7168 / 7680 / 28672, with and without 16 splits), with 50 back-to-back launches per shape. I did this with both NVCC 12.9.86 and 13.0.48.\nmain\ngave 0 bitwise mismatches in every case, and the regression test added in\n#448\nalso passes on\nmain\nwith both compilers (24 / 24).\nI also checked the SASS of\nmain\nfrom both compilers with a small script. It looks for writes to the A registers of an in-flight\nHGMMA\ngroup before the\nWARPGROUP.DEPBAR\nthat waits for it, and found none: ptxas puts the A fragments of consecutive stages in different registers. So the source-level race is real, but these two ptxas versions do not turn it into a hazard for these instantiations. That may explain why it is hard to reproduce, and it could still show up with other compiler versions.\nPerformance of\n#448\n.\nMedian of 3\nbench_kineto\nruns, NVCC 12.9, in \u00b5s:\nm, k, splits\nmain\n#448\ndouble-buffered A\n137, 28672, none\n106.5\n120.8 (+13%)\n111.4 (+5%)\n4096, 7680, none\n32.9\n36.2 (+10%)\n33.8 (+3%)\n4096, 7680, 16\n45.5\n38.0 (\u221216%)\n47.6 (+5%)\n8192, 28672, none\n123.5\n131.8 (+7%)\n125.2 (+1%)\nThe geometric mean over all 24 shapes versus\nmain\nis +2.8% for\n#448\nand +2.2% for the double-buffered variant (NVCC 13.0: +4.6% and +2.9%).\n#448\ncosts 8\u201313% on most shapes without splits, but it is about 16% faster on the\nk = 7680\n, 16-split shapes.\nThe double-buffered variant keeps two A register buffers selected by stage parity, and waits with one WGMMA group in flight (\nwarpgroup_wait<1>\n) before a buffer is reused. It fixes the race by construction and recovers most of the loss on the shapes without splits, but it does not get\n#448\n's gain on the 16-split shapes. So it is not clearly better overall. The patch is on\nLiRunGuo/DeepGEMM@sm90-hc-prenorm-double-buffered-a\nif it is useful.\nleevan\ncommented\non\nSep 23, 2026\nleevan\non Sep 23, 2026\nAuthor\nMore actions\n@LiRunGuo\ncool, maybe you can try with a H20. regarding the performance, I do have another version of double buffer which improves the performance.\nLiRunGuo\ncommented\non\nSep 29, 2026\nLiRunGuo\non Sep 29, 2026\nMore actions\n@leevan\nThanks for the pointer. Draft sampling dtype mismatch\nlogits_to_probs\ncomputes the draft distribution as:\np\n=\nsoftmax\n(\nlogits\n.\nfloat\n()\n/\nT\n)\nand uses that float32\np\nin the speculative acceptance ratio\nmin(1, q / p)\nand correction distribution. In effect, the draft token was drawn from a represented distribution\nr\n, but acceptance and correction were computed as if it came from\np\n.\nFor a one-token speculative step, with sample distribution\nr\nbut acceptance math using\np\n:\na_y = min(1, q_y / p_y)\nc_y = (q_y - p_y)_+ / sum_z (q_z - p_z)_+\nPr[out = y] = r_y a_y + (sum_x r_x (1 - a_x)) c_y\nWhen\nr = p\n, this collapses to the target distribution\nq\n. When\nr != p\n, it generally does not.\nA minimal non-degenerate example demonstrates the final marginal bias:\np = [0.3, 0.7]\nr = [0.30078125, 0.69921875]\nq = [0.4, 0.6]\n\na = [1, 0.6 / 0.7]\nc = [1, 0]\n\nPr[out = 0] = 0.30078125 + 0.69921875 * (1 - 0.6 / 0.7)\n            = 0.40066964\nq[0]        = 0.40000000\nThe exact bf16 error bound is not the important part of the fix, but the scale is enough to matter: bf16 has 7 explicit mantissa bits, spacing near 1 of\n2^-7 ~= 0.78%\n, and round-to-nearest error on the order of\n2^-8 ~= 0.39%\nfor normal-range values.\nThis PR changes\nsample_tokens\nto cast before temperature scaling and softmax:\nflat_logits\n=\nlogits\n.\nreshape\n(\n-\n1\n,\nvocab_size\n).\nfloat\n()\n/\ntemperature\nThat makes the sampled draft distribution match the\np\nused by rejection sampling.\n2. Warmup to cosine LR overshoot\nThis is a wrapper state-transition bug, not ordinary\nCosineAnnealingLR\nbehavior.\nAt the warmup/cosine handoff, the old wrapper delegated to the cosine scheduler's chainable\nget_lr()\npath with:\ncosine.last_epoch == 0\ncosine._is_initial == False\noptimizer.lr == warmup_peak\nThat is not the ordinary closed-form epoch-0 cosine value. The recursive update applies:\nLR = eta_min + 2 / (1 + cos(pi / T_max)) * (LR_current - eta_min)\nWith\neta_min = 0\nand\nLR_current = peak_lr\n, the transition becomes:\nLR_transition = 2 / (1 + cos(pi / T_max)) * peak_lr\nSince\ncos(pi / T_max) < 1\nfor\nT_max > 1\n, this is above the configured peak. Examples:\nT_max\nfactor\novershoot\n5\n1.10557\n+10.56%\n10\n1.02509\n+2.51%\n50\n1.00099\n+0.0988%\n100\n1.00025\n+0.0247%\nThis PR special-cases the handoff to return the configured peak/base LRs directly instead of calling the recursive\nget_lr()\nbranch at\nlast_epoch == 0\n. Expanding or slicing it cannot create cached-key columns:\ncausal:        [1, 1, seq_len, (k + 1) * seq_len]\nexpanded_mask: [B, 1, 1, seq_len]\nAdding those tensors fails on dim 3 for every cached step where\nkv_len != seq_len\n. This PR now extends the keep-mask by repeating the fixed chunk mask pattern until it reaches\nkv_len\n, then slices to\nkv_len\n. The `MoEEpCommunication` interface from #5532 is unchanged.\n\nIt also completes the deprecation started in #5532. No `MoEEpCommunication` backend builds on `MoeAlltoAll` or `MnnvlMoe` any more, so both classes are **removed** (breaking; see *Removal and migration* below). `NVLinkOneSidedAlltoAll` and `CakeAlltoAll` take over `MoeAlltoAll`'s `checkpoint_prepare` / `checkpoint_restore`.\n\n### What the new kernels bring\n\n- **CFT counted writes.** On Blackwell systems whose driver exports the CUDA logical-endpoint API, dispatch and combine can push payloads over the NVLink fabric with `fabric.try_put.counted`. The receiver then waits on hardware byte counters instead of per-round completion flags, and the CFT dispatch also fills the padding rows' expert ids itself. The logical endpoint is bound to the existing MNNVL workspace, so no extra memory is allocated.\n- **Up to 256 EP ranks** (was 64); the active-rank mask grows to four words.\n- **Workspace laid out by phase.** Round state, dispatch control and payload, and combine control, input and the CFT receive inbox are separate regions with fixed capacities, which every op validates.\n- **Routing and fan-out.**\n  - Invalid expert ids are skipped during routing.\n  - When `top_k > ep_size`, dispatch and combine fan out over a compact per-rank destination list.\n  - Receive counters are double-buffered by round parity; the CFT dispatch publishes them right after routing.\n- **Low-precision combine** pairs FP8 conversions.\n- **Timeouts** are chosen on the host per launch.\n\n### Python\n\n- `NVLinkOneSidedAlltoAll` drives the new JIT module (`moe_ep_nvlink_one_sided_alltoall`) directly.\n  - **Workspace sharing:** instances with the same layout share one workspace, which is freed when its last instance is destroyed. Instances on one workspace must run their rounds one after another; a dispatch while another instance's round awaits its combine raises.\n  - **CFT setup:** endpoint creation and exchange run over the EP group's `CommBackend`, so no MPI is involved. Every rank agrees on CFT before the layout is fixed, and a failure on any rank falls back to the fence path on all ranks.\n- `NVLinkOneSidedConfig` gains:\n  - `cft`: `None` uses CFT automatically where supported, for steps up to `cft_max_tokens_for_dispatch` / `cft_max_tokens_for_combine` tokens (128 each); `True` uses it on every supported step; `False` never uses it;\n  - `timeout_sec`: the bound on each wait for a peer;\n  - `enable_pdl`: programmatic dependent launch, `None` enabling it on SM90+ as before (also on `CakeAlltoAllConfig`).\n- `NVLinkOneSidedAlltoAll.active_rank_mask(ranks)` builds the 256-rank mask, and `cft_enabled` reports whether CFT is available to the instance.\n- **`CakeAlltoAll`** is now a standalone `MoEEpCommunication` (it used to subclass `NVLinkOneSidedAlltoAll`). The generated Cake kernels implement the protocol of the functional `moe_a2a_*` ops, which it calls with `backend=\"cake\"`; those ops are unchanged. `CakeAlltoAll` pins the combine region at the end of the workspace instead of using the offset each dispatch returns, which moves with the token count (the race #6376 fixed in `MoeAlltoAll`), and follows the same one-round-per-workspace rule.\n- `benchmarks/moe_ep/core/comm/bench_moe_ep_comm.py` gets `--cft {auto,on,off}`.\n- The module is in the AOT build list for SM90+.\n\n### Checkpointing\n\n`NVLinkOneSidedAlltoAll` and `CakeAlltoAll` gain `checkpoint_prepare()` and `checkpoint_restore(comm_backend)`, with the semantics `MoeAlltoAll` had (callers such as vLLM used to reach them through the former `.alltoall` accessor):\n\n- **Prepare:** releases the physical MNNVL memory and keeps the virtual addresses reserved.\n- **Restore:** remaps the memory over a fresh `CommBackend` and re-initializes the workspace. CUDA graphs captured before the checkpoint replay correctly afterwards.\n- **Shared rules:** both calls are collective, and repeated calls do nothing.\n- **CFT endpoints:**\n  - `NVLinkOneSidedAlltoAll` also releases its CFT logical endpoints before the memory and recreates them afterwards.\n  - Launches bake the endpoint IDs into their kernel parameters, so the endpoints keep their ID block reserved across the checkpoint (`moe_a2a_cft_release_endpoints`) and are recreated under the same IDs.\n  - Restore verifies the IDs and raises if they changed.\n- **CftLeManager fix:** it now tracks imported peer endpoints explicitly. It used to treat ID 0 as unset, and ID blocks start at 0, so the import of rank 0's endpoint was never destroyed. Two independent causes; both are needed on current main.\n\n**1. Draft rows mirrored before the drafter writes them.** The MTP layers are HiSparse layers too, and HiSparse marks a page clean and releases it for all of its layers, target and draft, at once. Each step does:\n\n```\nstart_step \u2192 target forward \u2192 finish_forward \u2192 propose (drafter writes its rows)\n```\n\n`finish_forward` mirrored *all* layers to host, including draft layers whose rows `propose` had not written yet, and then reported the step's pages clean. The drafter's own per-layer mirror is skipped under FULL graphs, so the fresh draft rows never reached host. When the page's GPU block was reused, the drafter read stale host rows.\n\n**2. The residency resolver can read stale request ids** (regression from #59235). The resolver runs on the HiSparse copy stream, which outside PIECEWISE graphs waits only on `logical_topk_ready`, recorded right after the indexer. #59235 writes the masked request ids later, on the compute stream, so the resolver can read the previous call's ids. The MTP layer alternates four rows per request (draft prefill) with one (draft decode), so stale ids resolve draft rows against other requests' KV.\n\n## Changes\n\n- The speculator tags its draft attention layers (`AttentionLayerBase.is_draft_layer`); HiSparse binding marks their cache handles as draft layers.\n- `finish_forward` mirrors only target layers.\n- The next step's `start_step` first mirrors the previous step's draft-layer rows (the drafter has run by then), then submits that step's page transfers behind them on the same DMA stream, so a page is only reported clean after its draft rows are queued. They are queued before the step swaps host write events, so the new step's forward and host copies wait for them: by then the scheduler may have handed a finished request's GPU and host blocks to another request. No connector API changes (`wait_for_save` stays a no-op).\n- Build the resolver's masked request ids on the copy stream after its wait, into buffers owned by the HiSparse index group (moved from the generic `SparseMLAIndexGroup`); `swap_in` now requires the valid-row count.\n\n**Why not just move `finish_forward` after `propose`?** Outside FULL graphs the drafter re-prepares the draft handles with its own (decode-shaped) metadata, so a combined end-of-step mirror hits HiSparse's metadata consistency checks (`RuntimeError`) for every target/drafter graph-mode mix except FULL/FULL. Target and draft layers need to be mirrored at different points, which requires knowing which layers are draft layers.\n\n**Known limitation (follow-up).** A host block freed after step N (finished or preempted request) can be reallocated to a P/D import before step N's deferred copies land; NIXL writes are not ordered against the copy stream, so an imported request could, rarely, receive stale draft-layer rows (or, with the non-default lazy mirror mode, stale rows for all layers of a preempted request's spilled page). GPU writes and host copy-on-write are ordered: the next step waits for the deferred copies before its forward and host copies. The follow-up holds freed host blocks until the step's deferred writes are reported done.\n\n## Test Plan / Results\n\n**Unit:**\n- `test_draft_layer_rows_mirrored_after_drafter[FULL|NONE]` drives the real worker and checks that host draft rows equal the drafter's writes, with exactly one draft-layer copy and the page reported only after it. On main the FULL case fails.\n- `test_hisparse_resolver_reads_current_request_ids` (GPU) stalls the compute stream between `logical_topk_ready` and attention, then resolves four rows per request followed by one row per request plus a padding row. It fails on main and passes here.\n- H100: `test_sparse_mla_backends.py -k \"hisparse or index_group\"` 40 passed; HiSparse connector/worker tests pass.\n- `tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py`: the FULL-graph host-mirror check now verifies MTP rows when the next step's start mirrors them (it compared them right after `finish_forward`, before the drafter writes them) and requires the MTP layer to be detected as a draft layer. 4 passed (H100); fails if the speculator stops tagging its layers.\n\n**E2E, cause 1 (on the pre-#59235 base):** H200 2\u00d78, GLM-5.3 TP8/EP8 HiSparse decoder, MTP3, We separate the two with an information floor, the minimum expected rejection at a specified conditioning order; rejection above this floor is the model gap. Estimating both from target rollouts across four domains, four open-weight targets, and a frontier API target yields three findings. First, the all-parallel floor reaches 0.286 at the final slot on Qwen3-4B, limiting even the best proposal to 71% per-slot acceptance. "https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/issues/476", "title": "[Bug] SM90 `fp8_einsum(\"bhr,hdr->bhd\", a, b, d, c)` silently drops `c` and returns `a @ b.T`", "body": "## Description\n\nOn SM90, `deep_gemm.fp8_einsum(\"bhr,hdr->bhd\", a, b, d, c=c)` returns $d = a \\cdot b^\\top$ instead of $d = c + a \\cdot b^\\top$. No error is raised, and the output looks like a normal result. The same happens when `d` and `c` are the same tensor (in-place accumulation). On SM100 the result is correct.\n\n[The README's convention](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/README.md?plain=1#L63) is `D = C + A @ B` (\"`fp8_gemm_nt` will do a `D = C + A @ B.T`\"), and `fp8_einsum` accepts `c` on every architecture. `\"bhr,hdr->bhd\"` is the only `fp8_einsum` expression that runs on SM90, so any caller that accumulates through it on Hopper gets a wrong result.\n\n## Environment\n\n- H100 80GB HBM3 (sm_90), driver 580.126.09, CUDA 13.0 (nvcc V13.0.88), torch 2.9.1+cu130.\n- DeepGEMM `main` 1fc9c66, CUTLASS f3fde58, built with `./develop.sh`.\n\n## Root Cause\n\nThe host prepares `d` for an accumulating kernel, but on SM90 it launches a kernel that only stores:\n\n1. `fp8_einsum` passes `c` to `fp8_bmm` ([einsum.hpp L276](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/csrc/apis/einsum.hpp#L276)), which calls `gemm::early_return` ([L230](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/csrc/apis/einsum.hpp#L230)). It copies `c` into `d`, expecting the kernel to add into `d` ([gemm.hpp L49\u2013L51](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/csrc/apis/gemm.hpp#L49-L51)):\n\n   ```cpp\n   // With accumulation, do copy before GEMM (assuming the GEMM kernel does not support different C/D)\n   if (c.has_value() and not is_cd_same)\n       d.copy_(c.value());\n   ```\n\n2. On SM90, `fp8_bmm` calls `sm90_fp8_bmm` ([einsum.hpp L247](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/csrc/apis/einsum.hpp#L247)), which launches `sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d_impl`. It sets `with_accumulation = c.has_value()` in the `GemmDesc` ([sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d.hpp L300](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/csrc/jit_kernels/impls/sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d.hpp#L300)), but the flag is not a template argument of the kernel ([L36\u2013L61](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/csrc/jit_kernels/impls/sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d.hpp#L36-L61)), and the kernel writes `D` with a plain TMA store ([sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d.cuh L434](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/deep_gemm/include/deep_gemm/impls/sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d.cuh#L434)):\n\n   ```cpp\n   if constexpr (kGemmType == GemmType::Batched) {\n       cute::SM90_TMA_STORE_3D::copy(&tensor_map_d, smem_ptr,\n                                     n_idx, m_idx, scheduler.current_group_idx);\n   ```\n\n   This overwrites the `c` that step 1 copied into `d`. For comparison, `sm90_bf16_gemm` passes `with_accumulation` to its kernel as `kWithAccumulation` and switches the store to a reduce-add.\n\n3. The other launcher of the same kernel, `sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d` (used by `fp8_gemm_nt`), rejects `c` ([sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d.hpp L81](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/csrc/jit_kernels/impls/sm90_fp8_gemm_1d2d.hpp#L81)):\n\n   ```cpp\n   DG_HOST_ASSERT(not c.has_value() and d.scalar_type() == torch::kBFloat16);\n   ```\n\n   `sm90_fp8_bmm` has no such check.\n\n`tests/test_einsum.py` passes `c` to `fp8_einsum` only on SM100 ([L183](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/blob/1fc9c66975ee322d628b3288534ca0e9ce12a64d/tests/test_einsum.py#L183)), so the SM90 path with `c` is untested.\n\n## Reproduction\n\n`repro.py`:\n\n```python\nimport torch\nimport deep_gemm\nfrom deep_gemm.utils.math import per_block_cast_to_fp8, per_token_cast_to_fp8\n\ntorch.manual_seed(0)\nb, h, r, d = 128, 8, 4096, 1024\nx = torch.randn(b, h, r, device='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)\ny = torch.randn(h, d, r, device='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)\nx_fp8, x_sf = per_token_cast_to_fp8(x.view(-1, r), use_ue8m0=False)\ny_fp8, y_sf = zip(*(per_block_cast_to_fp8(y[i], use_ue8m0=False) for i in range(h)))\na_ = (x_fp8.view(b, h, r), x_sf.view(b, h, r // 128))\nb_ = (torch.stack(y_fp8), torch.stack(y_sf))\n\nab = torch.einsum('bhr,hdr->bhd', x.float(), y.float())\n# as large as a @ b.T, in the layout fp8_einsum requires for C: [h, b, d] viewed as [b, h, d]\nc = (ab.std() * torch.randn(h, b, d, device='cuda')).bfloat16().permute(1, 0, 2)\nd_out = torch.empty_like(c)\ndeep_gemm.fp8_einsum('bhr,hdr->bhd', a_, b_, d_out, c=c)\n\nrel_err = lambda ref: ((d_out.float() - ref).norm() / ref.norm()).item()\nprint(f'relative error vs c + a @ b.T: {rel_err(c.float() + ab):.3f}')   # expected: small\nprint(f'relative error vs a @ b.T:     {rel_err(ab):.3f}')               # actual: small\n```\n\n## Expected vs Actual\n\nExpected: `d_out` \u2248 `c + a @ b.T`, with a relative error at the FP8 level. SM89 is the first architecture below Hopper that has FP8 Tensor Cores.\n\nPreviously, SM80 and SM89 used the same path. The path required SM90 or higher for FP8. This was correct for SM80 because Ampere has no FP8 Tensor Cores. It was wrong for SM89. SM89 implements the instruction `mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k32.row.col.f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` (`QMMA.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3`). The change separates the two architectures and gives SM89 a real kernel.\n\n## Why\n\n- SM89 has FP8 Tensor Cores. It does not have the SM90 features (no TMA, no `mbarrier.try_wait.parity`, no WGMMA, no clusters). It could not reuse the SM90 or SM100 kernels. It fell back to BF16 through cuBLASLt.\n- FP8 users on Ada had to dequantize and run BF16. They lost about 2\u00d7 of Tensor Core throughput.\n- The shared SM80/SM89 path also gave wrong error messages. An SM89 user saw a message that did not apply to their GPU.\n\n## Design\n\nSM89 has no TMA and no asynchronous barriers. The kernel uses the pre-Hopper primitives.\n\n- It uses `mma.sync` (wrapped in `deep_gemm/mma/sm89.cuh`, with A/B/C fragment layouts documented) and `ldmatrix.x4` for operand staging.\n- It uses a multi-stage `cp.async` pipeline with a 128-byte XOR swizzle.\n- It uses a persistent block scheduler (one CTA per SM). Tiles walk in a loop.\n- It uses direct global stores because SM89 has no TMA store. It has an alignment-safe scalar tail. An MMA lane owns a pair of adjacent columns. For odd N the element offset of a row can be odd. A 2-element vector store is then illegal. This caused the original misaligned address failure.\n- Block K is fixed at 128 because of the per-128-channel scaling granularity. Pipeline depth and tile shapes come from a new cost model in `csrc/jit_kernels/heuristics/sm89.hpp`. The warp split uses one shared function `get_mma_sync_warps_n()`. Host heuristics and device code both call it so they cannot disagree.\n\nBoth SM90 SF recipes are supported:  \n`(1, 1, 128)` (per-token A and B scales) and  \n`(1, 128, 128)` (per-token A, one B scale per 128-column N block).  \nThe second recipe is the default when FP32 scales are used. SM89 uses the same FP32 SF layouts as SM90. The function `transform_sf_into_required_layout` was extended. It was not duplicated.\n\n## Scope\n\nSupported features:  \ndense FP8 GEMM, K-major (NT) operands only, FP32 and BF16 outputs, `D = C + A @ B`, ragged M/N, `k % 16 == 0`, both aliases (`fp8_fp4_gemm_nt`, `fp8_gemm_nt`, `fp4_gemm_nt`), and shape specialization.\n\nStill rejected (with an explicit message that names the requirement):  \ngrouped and K-grouped FP8, MN-major FP8 operands, FP4, custom epilogues, `alpha` scaling, PDL, and MQA/attention.  \nBF16 keeps its cuBLASLt fallback.\n\n## Incidental fixes\n\n- `set_pdl()` now panics below SM90. It no longer sets a flag that `griddepcontrol` cannot honour.  \n  `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()` is wrapped in a no-op below `__CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900` so the SF-layout kernels compile for SM89.\n- `call_cublaslt_api` used `CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_FAST_TF32` for non-FP32 operands. That mode only down-casts FP32 inputs to TF32. BF16/FP8 operands ran at TF32 precision by mistake. Now only FP32 inputs use that mode.\n- A new `DG_PANIC` macro throws always and carries a message.\n\n## Bug found during validation\n\nThe persistent loop primed its `cp.async` pipeline only in the prologue before the tile loop. It relied on a cross-tile tail load to prime the next tile. A tile\u2019s tail can only reach the stages that are already free of the current tile \u2014 prologue stages `p \u2208 [0, kNumStages-2-num_k_blocks]`. The next tile\u2019s K loop consumes `p = 0..num_k_blocks-1`. When `num_k_blocks < kNumStages-1` (example: `k=512`, 4 blocks, 8 stages) the high stages were never reloaded. The next tile read the previous tile\u2019s shared memory. Symptom: non-deterministic `nan` and values near 1e30. The problem appeared only for small M spread over many N tiles.\n\nThe fix extracts the prologue into `prime_pipeline()` and re-primes unconditionally after the epilogue. The re-prime is guarded by `cp_async_wait<0>()` and a `__syncthreads()`. `cp.async` completion is per-thread, so both are required before the stages can be reused. The change removes a prologue/epilogue overlap that was never correct. Measured cost is about 0\u20133.5 % (4096\u00b3: 2518 \u00b5s vs 2507 \u00b5s, within noise; 4096\u00d74096\u00d7512: 420 \u00b5s vs 405 \u00b5s).\n\n`tests/test_sm89.py` added the shapes `(1, 4096, 512)`, `(64, 4096, 512)` and `(128, 4096, 128)`. Reverting the fix makes these tests fail (34 failures). They are real regression tests.\n\n## Testing\n\nHardware: RTX 4060 Laptop (SM89, 24 SMs, 7.6 GiB), CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130.\n\n- `tests/test_sm89.py` \u2014 17 tests, OK from a cold JIT cache (~130 s).  \n  Covers both recipes \u00d7 both output dtypes \u00d7 accumulate \u00d7 12 shapes, explicit `recipe=(1,128,128)`, `recipe_a`/`recipe_b` pairs, entry-point aliases, c", "created_at": "2026-10-14T19:01:11Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-16T18:30:02Z", "fetched_at": "2026-10-20T12:14:23Z", "state": "open", "merged_at": null, "parent": null, "tags": ["h100", "throughput", "performance", "nvfp4"], "metadata": {"number": 474, "labels": [], "comments": 0, "state_reason": null}, "content_hash": "e9e726ee03fe75aa494d2982073d7cff644a759f6b2dc7cbce2a25919d9f2557", "rank": -2.6948185269722282}, {"id": "github:deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM:415:live-page", "source": "github", "kind": "resource", "url": "https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/pull/415", "title": "Fix SM90 k-grouped GEMM hang and silent corruption when TMA multicast clusters straddle group boundaries by shoemoney \u00b7 Pull Request #415 \u00b7 deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM \u00b7 GitHub", "body": "Conversation\nshoemoney\ncommented\nAug 24, 2026\n\u2022\nedited\nLoading\nUh oh!\nThere was an error while loading.\nPlease reload this page\n.\nCopy link\nCopy Markdown\nSM90\nk_grouped_fp8_gemm_nt_contiguous\n(and the BF16 k-grouped path, which shares the same candidate enumerator) can hang or silently produce wrong output when the heuristic enables TMA multicast with an odd per-group block grid.\nBug\nThe k-grouped scheduler lays the groups' block grids back-to-back. Above 128 tokens the weight is re-streamed per tile and the two-call path is about 1.3x faster, so callers should route larger token counts there; any positive `M` is accepted.\n\n## Semantics\n\nEvery rank receives bitwise the same `out`: the local partial is rounded to bf16 once (as the unfused chain does before its collective), the cross-rank sum is taken in fixed rank order in fp32, one final rounding. The files those PRs added that are still on `main` come to 4,441 files and 4.9M lines. Of those, 3,522 are C++/CUDA/PTX files with 4.1M lines.\n- A single PR routinely adds 10^4\u201310^5 lines. They also bloat the source distribution and the JIT cache, and they make regressions hard to bisect.\n\n## What is wrong\n\nExamples below are from `main` at 45d35e4e7.\n\n1. **Unused kernel instances.** Some sources are never registered, or cannot be reached from any dispatch path. Superseded generations were never deleted.\n2. **Near-duplicate kernels in separate files.** For example, `csrc/cake_trtllm_moe_allreduce_union` has 322 kernel files. After normalising the generated hash names and the architecture tag, only 48 distinct bodies remain.\n3. **Per-architecture copies.** Several families keep SM100a and SM103a trees that are identical or differ by a line or two. For example, in `flashinfer/experimental/kimi_k3_latent_moe` each SM100a/SM103a kernel pair differs only in the symbol name and one shared-memory address-conversion line.\n4. **Problem sizes and launch configs baked in as constants.** For example, `csrc/cake_minimax_h3_mxfp8_pre_attention` has 176 kernel files. That is 2 schedules \u00d7 44 values of `#define M` \u00d7 2 architectures.\n5. **Hard-coded strides and contiguity.** These force `.contiguous()` copies on the Python side, or make the op reject views.\n6. **Host overhead.**\n   - The Python hot path does per-call device-property queries, workspace allocations, tensor construction, and dict/string work.\n   - Generated C++ bindings carry their own device-guard classes, mutexes, and caches instead of using `tvm_ffi_utils.h`.\n7. **Other bloat.** Multi-thousand-line generated Python registries and dispatch tables, per-architecture generated dispatchers, large metadata JSON files, raw PTX blobs, and README benchmark dumps.\n\n## Plan\n\nThere are two tracks.\n\n**Fix the generator and exporter so new exports are lean by construction.**\n\n- One source per schedule, shared across architectures. The existing barrier-based `CustomAllreduce` uses two explicit cross-GPU NVLink barrier round-trips per call, which dominate latency for small tensors. The push protocol eliminates these barriers entirely by having each rank push its data to all remote GPUs via NVLink volatile stores and then polling locally for arrival using a positive-zero sentinel mechanism with double-buffered epoch alternation.\n\nThe new `PushAllReduce` communicator is inserted into the `CudaCommunicator` dispatch chain above the existing `CustomAllreduce` for messages below a dynamic size threshold (~720 KB at TP=8 on B200). Messages above this threshold continue to use the barrier-based path. No existing `CustomAllreduce` code is modified. The implementation includes a consolidated CUDA kernel header vendored from SGLang's proven push kernel with minimal macro substitutions (namespace, C++17 compatibility, AOT compilation guards), a C++ host-side manager class following vLLM patterns, torch custom op bindings, and a Python communicator wrapper with CUDA graph support.\n\nThe kernel uses all available SMs (vs 2 CTAs in the barrier-based approach), supports PDL (`griddepcontrol`) overlap on sm_90+ architectures, and avoids the `cudaMemcpy` to IPC staging buffer required by the barrier-based path in eager mode. CUDA graph safety is ensured by placing the epoch counter in device memory (read live during replay) with a fixed grid size equal to the SM count.\n\n## Performance Results\n\n| Configuration | Metric | Baseline | Patched | Delta | Change |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| DeepSeek-V4-Pro (8xB200, TP=8) | Throughput (tok/s) | 82.301 | 84.060 | +1.759 | **+2.14%** |\n| DeepSeek-V4-Pro (8xB200, TP=8) | TPOT (ms/tok) | 12.152 | 11.897 | -0.255 | **-2.09%** |\n| DeepSeek-V4-Flash (2xB200, TP=2) | Throughput (tok/s) | 127.035 | 130.905 | +3.870 | **+3.05%** |\n| DeepSeek-V4-Flash (2xB200, TP=2) | TPOT (ms/tok) | 7.873 | 7.640 | -0.233 | **-2.96%** |\n\nWorkload: decode, BS=1, ISL=4, OSL=33024, KV cache FP8. Baseline = same patched code with push allreduce disabled via env var (falls back to barrier-based `CustomAllreduce`).\n\nPer-call improvement on V4-Pro (122 allreduce calls per forward pass across 61 layers): ~2.09 us/call.\n\n## Correctness (lm_eval)\n\n| Configuration | Metric | Baseline | Patched | Delta | Status |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| DeepSeek-V4-Pro (8xB200, TP=8) | flexible-extract exact_match | 0.9515 | 0.9530 | +0.0015 | PASS |\n| DeepSeek-V4-Pro (8xB200, TP=8) | strict-match exact_match | 0.9515 | 0.9538 | +0.0023 | PASS |\n| DeepSeek-V4-Flash (2xB200, TP=2) | flexible-extract exact_match | 0.9598 | 0.9530 | -0.0068 | PASS |\n| DeepSeek-V4-Flash (2xB200, TP=2) | strict-match exact_match | 0.9606 | 0.9530 | -0.0076 | PASS |\n\nBenchmark: gsm8k 5-shot (1319 prompts). "https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58498", "title": "[Bugfix] Don't sync-police or retry FlashInfer all-reduce workspace creation in eager mode", "body": "## Purpose\n\nFix a nightly regression from #58197 (\"[Core] Disable JIT warmup in eager mode\").\n\nWith `--enforce-eager` the V2 `warmup_kernels` dummy forward is now skipped. The standalone FlashInfer all-reduce (`FlashInferAllReduce`, enabled by default through `VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=1`) creates its workspace lazily. The profile run uses large tensors that are above the FlashInfer size cap (e.g. 0.5 MB at TP8 or 2 MB at TP4 on H200), so it never touches the workspace. As a result, the workspace is first created inside the first real `execute_model`, which runs after `enable_gpu_sync_check()`. In CI (`VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error`), `flashinfer_comm.create_allreduce_fusion_workspace(...)` then raises `RuntimeError: GPU<->CPU sync detected` part-way through a collective. The failure is caught and returns `None`, and `get_fi_ar_workspace` does not remember it. The mnnvl attempt fails, the trtllm fallback fails, and the collective creation keeps getting retried. Each retry leaks partially created buffers, which leads to CUDA OOM, then a deadlock, then `TimeoutError: RPC call to sample_tokens timed out` and `EngineDeadError`.\n\nEvidence (nightly build 90589):\n- H200 LM Eval DeepSeek V3.2 TP8 (`--enforce-eager`): https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/90589#01a0ccda-d861-443c-bcb5-9c8b22260601. At 11:45:56 it logs `Failed to initialize FlashInfer All Reduce workspace: GPU<->CPU sync detected`, followed by repeated `Failed to initialize FlashInfer Allreduce norm fusion workspace with backend=trtllm`. OOM follows by 11:46:18 and the RPC timeout at 11:50:53.\n- B200 HiSparse (GLM-5.2-NVFP4 TP4), job `01a0cd35-9fed-4cff-a2be-b8c4ea5fb773` in the same build, fails the same way.\n- Passing build 90513 (before #58197) logs `Initialized FlashInfer Allreduce norm fusion workspace with backend=mnnvl` during warmup.\n- This is likely also behind the H100 Fault Tolerance E2E failure (`rank 0 did not report UNHEALTHY within 45s`) that #58318 is bisecting. That link is not verified.\n\n## Fix\n\nIn `vllm/distributed/device_communicators/flashinfer_all_reduce.py`:\n1. Wrap the one-time `create_allreduce_fusion_workspace` call in `gpu_sync_allowed()`. This covers both the regular and the quant workspace paths, since both go through `_create_workspace`. Setup syncs are expected here and are not a per-step cost.\n2. Remember a failed creation (`_fi_ar_workspace_failed` / `_fi_ar_quant_workspace_failed`) so a collective creation is never retried on every all-reduce call. `destroy_fi_ar_workspace()` resets both flags.\n\nI also considered creating the workspace eagerly before `enable_gpu_sync_check()` when warmup is skipped. That approach would have to guess the hidden size and dtype in the worker. It would also leave the retry-storm failure mode in place for any other lazy-creation failure. The change above is smaller and local to the module that owns the workspace.\n\n## Not a duplicate\n\n- `gh pr list --state open --search \"flashinfer all reduce workspace\"`, `\"58197\"`, `\"gpu_sync_allowed\"`, `\"flashinfer allreduce eager\"` and `\"enforce-eager warmup\"` returned no PR that fixes this.\n- #58318 is a DNM CI-bisect probe that reverts #58197. It is not a fix.\n\n## Test Plan / Results\n\nGPU checks ran on an idle 8\u00d7H200 host (GPUs 0-3), using the nightly image `public.ecr.aws/q9t5s3a7/vllm-ci-postmerge-repo:de6674b0023b...` (the same image as build 90589). hierarchical allreduce for PCIe-only multi-island boxes", "body": "## Purpose\n\nOn PCIe-only boxes whose GPUs form multiple islands \u2014 e.g. 2\u00d74 A100/A800, where GPU0-3 and GPU4-7 are each PIX-connected and the two halves are bridged by the CPU interconnect \u2014 `CustomAllreduce` is unavailable (`is_fully_connected` is false) and every allreduce falls to the NCCL ring, which crosses the slow inter-island link repeatedly. Profiling DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 decode on an 8\u00d7A800 box put **allreduce at 68.6% of decode GPU time** (292 \u00b5s/call at decode shapes), far ahead of attention (2.3%) or the MoE GEMMs.\n\nThis adds an opt-in island-aware communicator. It is off unless the operator supplies an explicit island partition, so nothing changes for existing deployments.\n\n## Design\n\nEnabled with `VLLM_HIER_ALL_REDUCE=\"0,1,2,3;4,5,6,7\"`. Two Triton kernels share one set of IPC-registered buffers and dispatch on message size:\n\n- **one-shot** (< 24576 elements): publish the input, reduce the island over direct P2P reads, then one cross-island exchange. Two sync rounds, 4n remote bytes.\n- **two-shot** (\u2265 24576): reduce-scatter within the island, exchange only the `1/island_size` shard across islands, allgather. Three sync rounds, 7n/4 remote bytes \u2014 and only `n/island_size` crosses the slow link instead of `n`.\n\nThree details are load-bearing and worth calling out for review:\n\n1. **Push-based signalling.** PCIe has no native remote atomics, and having a reader poll a remote flag costs a PCIe round trip per spin. Writers instead store sequence tokens into the *reader's* local flag array and readers spin on local memory only, with `fence.acq_rel.sys` for ordering. Same shape as the existing CUDA custom-allreduce kernels.\n2. **Device-side sequence counters.** A host-supplied token would be baked into a CUDA graph and replay out of order, so the token comes from a device-side fetch-and-increment. Buffers then alternate by token parity, which makes it impossible for a rank that has lapped a slow peer to overwrite data the peer is still reading (a two-call lap is blocked by the flag waits).\n3. **Stripe CTA partitioning in the two-shot kernel.** CTA *k* owns slice *k* of *every* shard rather than one contiguous range, so a reader CTA always waits on the same CTA index of its peers across all three phases. That removes the need for a grid-wide barrier, which Triton has no primitive for.\n\nNote the IPC buffers are allocated and mapped through `cudaIpcOpenMemHandle` with the importing device current, rather than via torch's `_new_shared_cuda`: torch opens IPC handles inside the *owner's* device context, so the mapping is never made peer-accessible to the importing device's kernels \u2014 `copy_()` works but a kernel dereference is an immediate IMA, and `cudaDeviceEnablePeerAccess` does not retroactively fix an already-imported handle.\n\n## Not a duplicate of\n\n- **#36834 (Added Hierarchical all reduce)** \u2014 that is a *node-level* hierarchy for multi-node inference: intra-node NVLink custom allreduce plus inter-node RDMA through UCCL-EP. This PR is single-node and hierarchical *within* the box, over PCIe islands, on hardware that has no NVLink at all. No overlap in code or target.\n- **#44891 (push-based allreduce for small tensor reductions)** \u2014 shares the push/poll idea but is a flat (non-hierarchical) protocol in CUDA C++ targeting NVLink (threshold tuned on B200). This is a two-level algorithm in Triton for PCIe-island topologies. They compose: that PR's dispatch entry is above `CustomAllreduce`, this one is likewise independent and gated behind an explicit env.\n- **#39633 (Fix PCIe custom-allreduce eligibility on >2 GPU topologies)** \u2014 that reuses the *existing* barrier-based kernel on PCIe. I tried exactly that on this hardware first (the P2P access matrix is fully connected here, so the NVLink-only gate looked like policy rather than capability). It runs at 21 \u00b5s but returns **numerically wrong results** at `world_size=8` (max error 1.5 to `inf` against an NCCL reference), so I abandoned that route and wrote a separate kernel instead. Details posted on that PR \u2014 it may be worth verifying on SM120 before enabling.\n\n## Test plan\n\nNew `tests/distributed/test_hier_all_reduce.py` checks the communicator against `torch.distributed.all_reduce` across sizes that straddle the one-shot/two-shot threshold in both directions, plus a size that is not a multiple of the CTA tiling to exercise the masked tails. "https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57042", "title": "[Kernel] Accumulate ranks in absolute order in 2-stage custom all-reduce", "body": "## Purpose\n\n`cross_device_reduce_2stage` rotates the rank pointers, so each partition's owner starts its sum at its own rank. `cross_device_reduce_1stage` sums ranks in absolute order `0..N-1`. Both reduce through the same `packed_reduce`, which accumulates into float32 (`csrc/custom_collective_common.cuh:87`, `:323-330`). When those partial sums round, the two kernels can return different bits for the same all-reduce \u2014 and the choice between them is made by message size (`csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:298-307`: 1-stage below 512 KiB at \u22644 ranks and 256 KiB at \u22648, 2-stage above).\n\n(Line numbers are at main `b49c921a27`, this PR's base; the comment added here shifts the `.cuh` ones after line 47 by 2 on this branch.)\n\nThe rotation also makes 2-stage output depend on the total tensor size, even with no switch between kernels. This was independently measured by @curvedinf ([comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57042#issuecomment-5686335910)). `part = size / ngpus` moves the ownership boundaries whenever the size changes (`csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:38-40`), and each owner starts its sum at its own rank (`:45-48`). In their on-GPU in-vitro run of the unmodified kernels at 4 ranks and fp32, 14.86% of the elements of a 1664\u00d75120 tensor differ bitwise from the same rows of its 2048\u00d75120 parent. Both sizes are above the 512 KiB threshold, so this comes from a chunked-prefill geometry change alone. The 1-stage control on the same data is bit-identical, which pins the cause to the rotation this PR removes.\n\nThis PR makes the 2-stage kernel read the rank pointers in absolute order, so both kernels produce identical bits whichever one the heuristic selects, and 2-stage output no longer depends on the tensor size. The direction was proposed by @sfeng33 in the review of #50505; this is that change, split out and self-contained against main. cc @sfeng33\n\n**The change** is one line in `csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh`: `ptrs[i] = (const P*)_dp->ptrs[target]` \u2192 `_dp->ptrs[i]`.\n\nOnly `ptrs` loses the rotation. `tmps[i]` must keep it: `tmp_out = tmps[0]` has to be the rank's own scratch buffer, and the stage-2 gather indexes `tmps` with the same `(rank + i)` rotation. De-rotating both would make every rank write its stage-1 results into rank 0's scratch region. The code comment records this.\n\n**Why the kernels then agree bit-for-bit.** For every element, both compute `downcast(((up(x0) + up(x1)) + ...) + up(xN-1))` through the same float32 accumulator. There are no partial sums on the 2-stage path: each partition's owner computes the full N-term sum, and stage 2 only copies already-downcast values. Once the order matches, every operation matches.\n\n**Effect outside batch invariance.** This changes 2-stage output bit patterns for all runs, not only under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`. Before and after, each result sums the same terms through the same float32 accumulator; only the order of the additions differs. How often bits actually change depends on the data and dtype: in the CPU emulation below, plain random fp16/bf16 inputs changed no elements and fp32 inputs changed ~32% (31.28% on GPU in @curvedinf's run, below). No existing test asserts bit-exact 2-stage output: the custom all-reduce tests either run at TP=2, which always selects 1-stage, or force 1-stage (`test_custom_allreduce_chunked`), and the bit-exact all-gather/reduce-scatter tests never dispatch `allreduce()`.\n\n**Prior art, and why this is a separate PR.** #52231 by @mawong-amd already contains this same one-line change, with `ptrs` de-rotated and `tmps` kept rotated. It is part of a 36-file PR adding batch invariance on ROCm, which describes the change as making 2-stage batch-invariant and keeps that path disabled on CUDA pending tuning. This PR splits out only the kernel line, with a 4-rank differential test, so it can be reviewed and land on its own. If #52231 lands first, this PR reduces to the test. cc @mawong-amd\n\n#56358 also targets fixed-order TP reduction, but through an opt-in Python gather-and-sum path (`VLLM_TP_FIXED_ORDER_ALLREDUCE`); it doesn't touch this kernel. In this paper, \"fully generated\" refers to code provenance: implementation changes were produced and applied as agent-proposed diffs; validation relied on agent-run builds, tests, and differential checks, without per-change manual diff review. It implements a PyTorch-style eager tensor library with a C++20 core (CPU+CUDA), a torch-like Python overlay via nanobind, and an experimental Node.js/TypeScript interface. Unlike thin bindings, VIBETENSOR includes its own tensor/storage system, schema-lite dispatcher, reverse-mode autograd, CUDA runtime (streams/events/graphs), a stream-ordered caching allocator with diagnostics, and a stable C ABI for dynamically loaded operator plugins. We view this release as a milestone for AI-assisted software engineering: it shows coding agents can generate a coherent deep learning runtime spanning language bindings down to CUDA memory management, validated primarily by builds and tests. We describe the architecture, summarize the workflow used to produce and validate the system, and evaluate the artifact. The image and native KV-offload backend move from `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc24` to `release:1.3.0a0.dev202610151219`.\n\n**Search space (6 \u2192 9 points)**\n\n| Point | Prefill | Decode | Conc | Decode batch | Nodes |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1P1D | 1\u00d7 DEP1 | 1\u00d7 TEP2, on the prefill node | 38, 48 | 8 | 1 |\n| 1P1D | 1\u00d7 DEP1 | 1\u00d7 TEP2, on the prefill node | 45 | 4 | 1 |\n| 1P2D | 1\u00d7 TEP4 | 2\u00d7 TEP8 | 48 | 4 | 5 |\n| 1P4D | 1\u00d7 TEP4 | 4\u00d7 TEP8 | 38 | 1 | 9 |\n| 1P4D | 1\u00d7 TEP4 | 4\u00d7 TEP8 | 38 | 4 | 9 |\n| 2P3D | 2\u00d7 TEP4 | 3\u00d7 TEP8 | 136 | 4 | 8 |\n| 3P1D | 3\u00d7 DEP4 | 1\u00d7 DEP16 | 565 | 8 | 7 |\n| 3P2D | 3\u00d7 DEP4 | 2\u00d7 DEP4 | 704 | 32 | 5 |\n\nThe 1P7D, 2P2D and 2P3D TEP2/TEP8 points are removed. The two 1P1D batch-8 concurrencies share one override. All points keep `dram-utilization: 0.609524` (128 GiB per rank).\n\n**Engine and env**\n- Dynamo installs from the `1.6.0.dev20261010` wheel instead of `cquil11/dynamo` revision `2cbbdc86`. The `dynamo-router` version is now `1.6.0.dev20261010`.\n- `publish_events_and_metrics: false` becomes `publish_metrics: true`, so workers get `--publish-metrics` with KV events off. Both roles set `enable_iter_perf_stats: true`, `iter_perf_stats_interval: 40` and `kv_cache_config.iteration_stats_interval: 40`, so the `trtllm_kv_cache_utilization` metrics are produced and scraped.\n- TEP4 prefill uses `max_num_tokens: 32768` with compile capture up to 32768. 1P1D decode uses the `TRTLLM` MoE backend, and both 1P1D roles set `cache_transceiver_config.kv_cache_bounce_size_mb: 2048`. 3P2D decode `free_gpu_memory_fraction` goes from 0.8 to 0.85.\n- New env on both roles: `ENROOT_ALLOW_DEV`, `TLLM_PROFILE_LOG_RANKS=all`, `TRTLLM_KV_TRANSFER_NUM_THREADS=8`, and `rc` added to `UCX_TLS`. Prefill adds `TRTLLM_SKIP_KV_CACHE_ESTIMATION=1`, and 1P1D adds `TRT_LLM_DISABLE_LOAD_WEIGHTS_IN_PARALLEL=1`.\n- `TLLM_SPEC_DECODE_FORCE_NUM_ACCEPTED_TOKENS` is not set in the recipe; the launcher injects 3.80 from the golden acceptance length (MTP 6 drafts: 4.80 \u2212 1 = 3.80).\n\n**Frontend and benchmark**\n- The frontend stays on the head node, sets `router-session-affinity-ttl-secs: 14400` and drops the explicit `active-*-threshold: None` arguments.\n- Benchmark env: `AIPERF_HTTP_X_DYNAMO_SESSION_ID_FROM_CORRELATION_ID=true`, `AIPERF_USE_DYNAMO_CONV_AWARE_ROUTING=0`, `AIPERF_REQUIRED_SERVER_METRIC_PREFIX=trtllm_kv_cache_utilization`, and `WEKA_LOADER_OVERRIDE=semianalysis_cc_traces_weka_062126_256k`.\n- The benchmark client runs on the last decode node (`benchmark.placement.node: last_decode`).\n\n#3971 changes the same config key; this PR is independent of it.\n\n<details>\n<summary>AI model disclosure</summary>\n\nPrepared with Claude Code using `claude-opus-5-5` (Claude Opus 5.5). existing native sparse-decode API and dispatch remain unchanged. The new\npath is explicitly restricted to SM90 and is not enabled automatically.\nNote\nAlternative host-offload path (not part of this pr):\nThe packed interface also enables a separate offload path in which gathering and packing are performed on the host, followed by transferring only the packed selected-KV workspace to the device. In this case, the full KV caches of the shared layers no longer need to remain resident in HBM. This can substantially expand KV-cache capacity.\nSince this implementation introduces a compile-time packed-KV specialization in the existing SM90 sparse decode kernel, I\u2019d appreciate maintainers\u2019 guidance on whether you prefer the current shared-kernel approach, a policy/loader-based abstraction, or a separate packed-kernel implementation; I\u2019m happy to restructure it in a follow-up revision based on your feedback.\nMotivation\nGLM-5.2 can share selected physical indices across multiple MLA layers. When\nthose indices are available before the layer that consumes them, the runtime\ncan move sparse address resolution and KV gathering into an earlier overlap\nwindow.\nThe attention kernel can then read a contiguous packed workspace instead of\nrepeatedly:\nloading and validating physical indices;\ntranslating indices into page and in-page coordinates;\nconstructing unrelated global addresses; and\ngathering NoPE, scale, and RoPE components from the paged cache.\nPacking and attention are intentionally separate operations so a runtime can\noverlap packing with preceding work such as MoE communication.\nWhat changed\nSM90 packing kernel\npack_selected_kv\ncopies each selected 656-byte V3.2 record byte-for-byte:\n512-byte FP8 E4M3 NoPE data;\n16-byte FP32 scales; and\n128-byte BF16 RoPE data.\nThe packer writes an opaque 64-token tile-major workspace. It supports a valid\nselected-index prefix described by\ntopk_length\nand zero-fills invalid suffix\nrecords.\nCallers may provide reusable contiguous\nuint8\nstorage using\nget_packed_kv_workspace_size\n.\nPacked attention specialization\nThe packed H=64 and H=128 instantiations reuse FlashMLA's existing:\nWGMMA and dequantization pipeline;\nonline softmax;\nDSM clustering for H=128;\nsplit accumulation;\nepilogue; and\ncombine kernel.\nThe specialization replaces the sparse index/page/gather loader with direct\ntile-major loads and preserves partial-tail masking.\nScheduler policy\nH=128 uses the same scheduler as native sparse decode.\nH=64 uses the compact request-local scheduler selected by the L20X\nexperiments. For the measured full-prefix\ntopk=2048\n, 132-SM\nB*S_q=16\nregime, it falls back to the faster native scheduler.\nThis scheduler is used only by the opt-in packed helper and does not change\nnative sparse decode. The benchmark includes an identical-scheduler control to\nisolate the packed-load kernel gain.\nPython API\nThis PR adds:\nget_packed_kv_workspace_size\nget_packed_mla_metadata\npack_selected_kv\nflash_mla_with_packed_kvcache\nSupported scope\nThe initial path is intentionally limited to:\nSM90;\nV3.2 FP8 sparse KV records;\nd_qk=576\n;\nd_v=512\n;\nH in {64, 128}\n;\nMQA KV; and\ntop-k capacity divisible by 64.\nThe API fails closed for unsupported architectures and shapes. Now the wait sits between item k+1's QK(0)/QK(1) and its first PV, so the epilogue overlaps the next item's first QK. Only the last item of a CTA keeps the end-of-item wait.\n\n**D-U2.** Softmax now writes P as E4M3 into two 128B-swizzled K-major SMEM tiles, guarded by a new `p_free` barrier. Before, P aliased part of the FP32 score tile in TMEM. The MMA warp now issues QK(pair+1) before PV(pair), so the next softmax step overlaps PV(pair).\n\n**D-U2b.** QK-ahead order removes the implicit \"PV(s, p\u22121) is done\" edge that `s_full(p)` used to carry. Correction therefore now waits on `p_free[s]` before the TMEM rescale of pair >= 1. The 4-stage KV ring (sm_100a) exposes the race. The sm_103a text carried the same latent race, so D-U2b is in both texts.\n\n**S2.** Each of the 8 warps selects its local top-16 with a bitonic network (`_merge_warp_top16`), and warp 0 merges the 8 \u00d7 16 candidates with the same network. This replaces 16 rounds of CTA-wide argmax. Ties break by index, the same as in the reference, and dynamic barriers per CTA drop from 19 to 2.\n\n**Tradix v2.** Odd segments are visited as `j ^ (seg & 1)`, so the two half-warps no longer alias banks. The candidate stride is padded from 64 to 65 u64 and the output-count stride from 16 to 17. The comparator only compared tileK / unroll / tileM / tileN / scheduler, so many configs tied, and `std::sort` ordered the ties by its input, i.e. by the cubin manifest. #6726 only reordered pre-existing kernels in `flashinferMetaInfo.h`, and that moved the default onto slower tie-mates:\n\n- NVFP4 FC2 (`m=1 n=8192 k=1280`): the unsplit `c1x1x1` kernel (0.071 ms) was replaced by its `splitK3` tie-mate (0.135 ms). As a result `cmp(a, b)` and `cmp(b, a)` could disagree. With Static / Persistent / Persistent-split-K tie-mates near the SM count this forms a cycle, so the comparator was not a strict weak ordering, and split-K could still be the default in an input-order-dependent way.\n\nThis PR makes the order total and manifest-independent:\n\n1. **Prefer fewer `mNumSlicesForSplitK` slices**, placed before the scheduler tier. Split-K is still a candidate for the autotuner, which receives the full list.\n2. **Make the scheduler tier symmetric.** Its CTA estimate drops split-K and clusters, so it depends only on the tile shape, which both sides share at that tier. The tier also only decides Persistent vs non-Persistent.\n3. **Prefer deeper A/B pipelines** (`mNumStagesA`, then `mNumStagesB`).\n4. **Break the remaining ties with `strcmp(mFunctionName)`**, which is unique per manifest. Neither `std::stable_sort` nor a tie-break on the config index would help, because both still follow manifest order.\n\nOnly configs that the existing tiers left tied change order.\n\n### Performance (untuned default, `--autotune` off)\n\n`benchmarks/flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe` (or `trtllm_fp8_block_scale_moe`) `--routing_method renormalize --activation-type Swiglu --random_seed 42 --use_cuda_events`, median ms, one process per run. "https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41639", "title": "feat(amd): add native GLM MXFP4 Triton Gluon MoE backend", "body": "## Motivation\r\n\r\nGLM-5.2/5.3 decode on MI355X spends a material part of each step in the MoE layer. The existing runner boundary receives already-materialized top-k IDs and weights, so a model-specific kernel cannot optimize across router projection, top-k, route sorting, expert scheduling, activation quantization, routed experts, and the shared expert.\r\n\r\nThis PR adds an **explicit, strict, whole-layer Triton Gluon MoE backend** for the audited GLM Quark MXFP4 contract. Its main optimization is not a standalone faster top-k operation: the selected routes directly become the expert schedule, removing the generic `topk_ids -> moe_sorting -> expert GEMM` handoff.\r\n\r\nThe backend is opt-in and fail-closed. `auto` never selects it, unsupported contracts raise before execution, and a requested Gluon path never silently falls back to AITER or another MoE runner.\r\n\r\n## Modifications\r\n\r\n### 1. What this adds\r\n\r\n- `gluon` as a `MoeRunnerBackend` choice.\r\n- A reusable whole-layer `GluonMoeBackend` interface with model-specific binding, eager weight preparation, execution, and output ABI validation.\r\n- A GLM-5.2/5.3 implementation for serialized Quark W4A4 MXFP4 target experts and the audited BF16 NextN expert layout on gfx950.\r\n- Shape-family kernels for decode, speculative verification, and prefill, including continuous TP4/EP1 and TP8/EP1 coverage through a 32K prefill chunk.\r\n- TP/EP-aware shared-expert handling and reuse of SGLang's existing post-expert collective/finalization path.\r\n\r\nEnable the target and speculative paths explicitly:\r\n\r\n```bash\r\n--moe-runner-backend gluon \\\r\n--speculative-moe-runner-backend gluon\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 2. Kernel design\r\n\r\nThe optimized layer owns this model-specific sequence:\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nflowchart LR\r\n    subgraph A[\"Current SGLang + AITER boundary\"]\r\n        A0[\"BF16 hidden states\"] --> A1[\"router GEMM\"]\r\n        A1 --> A2[\"M x 256 logits\"]\r\n        A2 --> A3[\"biased sigmoid top-8\"]\r\n        A3 --> A4[\"dense IDs + weights\"]\r\n        A4 --> A5[\"generic moe_sorting<br/>count, bucket, pad, publish metadata\"]\r\n        A5 --> A6[\"quantize + GEMM1 + activation + GEMM2\"]\r\n        A6 --> A7[\"shared expert + add\"]\r\n    end\r\n\r\n    subgraph G[\"GLM Triton Gluon whole-layer path\"]\r\n        G0[\"BF16 hidden states\"] --> G1[\"router projection + input quant work<br/>co-scheduled in one launch grid\"]\r\n        G1 --> G2[\"fixed 256-expert sigmoid top-8\"]\r\n        G2 --> G3{\"active-token family\"}\r\n        G3 -->|\"tiny M\"| G4[\"selection/expert CTAs share a launch;<br/>expert CTAs recompute the needed route rank\"]\r\n        G3 -->|\"medium M\"| G5[\"selection directly emits expert tickets,<br/>sorted routes, and job descriptors\"]\r\n        G3 -->|\"large M\"| G6[\"chunk histogram + prefix/scatter<br/>and bucketed grouped projections\"]\r\n        G4 --> G7[\"MXFP4 experts + shared expert\"]\r\n        G5 --> G7\r\n        G6 --> G7\r\n    end\r\n```\r\n\r\nImportant details:\r\n\r\n- **Tiny M:** the router uses split-K CDNA4 MFMA work to expose enough CTAs on MI355X. Selection is compile-time specialized for 256 experts/top-8. The up-projection launch consumes the selected route directly instead of waiting for a generic sort.\r\n- **Medium M:** top-k appends routes directly to expert buckets and publishes the descriptors consumed by the expert projection.\r\n- **Large M:** chunked counting, prefix/scatter, and bucketed projections cover prefill shapes. The 32K family splits large routed-partial/code buffers so every gfx950 buffer address remains below the 4-GiB window.\r\n- **Quantization:** router projection and activation quantization are independent CTAs in the same launch grid; this removes a host launch and lets both work classes occupy the device together. They are not incorrectly described as a single CTA reading the input once.\r\n- **Shared expert:** TP/EP1 target execution consumes SGLang's normal appended shared-expert representation (257 experts). EP and NextN keep the native shared expert and add it before SGLang's existing collective.\r\n\r\nThe isolated measurements below show that standalone top-k is approximately tied with AITER. The useful difference is the producer/consumer boundary:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nAITER: router -> top-k metadata -> generic MoE sort -> expert work\r\nGluon: router/quant -> top-k becomes the expert schedule -> expert work\r\n```\r\n\r\n### rocprofiler-sdk kernel decomposition\r\n\r\nTo separate GPU work from Python/dispatcher/launch overhead, the full TP8/EP1 MoE call was profiled at PR HEAD `317b7156d` with rocprofiler-sdk 1.1.0 (`--kernel-trace --marker-trace --stats`). The specific fix\n> (`cache_aware`) is not yet validated end-to-end; I am running that now and\n> will post numbers before marking this ready.\n\n## Why\n\n`dsv4 fp4 mi355x vllm TP8/DPA mtp c128` reaches a **90.5%** GPU prefix cache hit\nrate against a **95.5%** theoretical ceiling, while the matching ATOM point\nreaches **92.4%** against **95.9%**.\n\n- vLLM: [run 34774626435 / job 103780081837](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/34774626435/job/103780081837)\n- ATOM: [run 33376779864 / job 99523226161](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/33376779864/job/99523226161)\n\nNormalising against each run's own ceiling, ATOM converts 96.4% of the\ntheoretically cacheable tokens into hits and vLLM only 94.7%.\n\n## Root cause\n\nUnder `--data-parallel-size 8` each DP rank is a separate engine with its own KV\npool (`GPU KV cache size: 6,259,837 tokens` x8) and its own prefix cache. A\nrequest only hits if it lands on the rank that already holds its prefix.\n\nThe launcher pins sessions with `--policy consistent_hash` plus\n`AIPERF_HTTP_X_SESSION_ID_FROM_CORRELATION_ID=1`. That works exactly as written\n\u2014 `router.log` shows session keys spread evenly over the 8 ranks (10.4%\u201315.9%\nof sessions each). The problem is the choice of key.\n\nJoining the run's `profile_export.jsonl` against `router.log`:\n\n| | |\n|---|---|\n| trajectories (`root_correlation_id` / `source_trace_id`) | 216 |\n| distinct `x_correlation_id` values used as routing keys | 1,440 |\n| requests at `agent_depth` 1 (sub-agent branches) | 4,707 / 7,569 |\n| trajectories scattered over 2\u20138 DP ranks | **99 / 216 (45.8%)** |\n| trajectories scattered over all 8 ranks | 13 (6.0%) |\n| prompt tokens belonging to a split trajectory | **446M / 819M (54.5%)** |\n\nThe agentic trace fans one trajectory out into several sub-agent branches that\ninherit the parent's context. Each branch gets its own correlation ID, so\n`consistent_hash` sends it to a different rank, and that rank has to prefill the\nshared prefix into its own pool again.\n\nPer-rank hit rates track this: 87.1% / 87.5% / 89.4% / 90.3% / 90.4% / 91.6% /\n91.9% / 92.3% (volume-weighted 90.48%, matching the reported 90.5%).\n\n## Evidence for the mechanism\n\nOn an 8xMI355X box I brought up the same config locally (same args, same\n`block size 256` / `DEEPSEEK_SPARSE_SWA`, 6,336,403 tokens per rank) and replayed\na synthetic workload shaped like the trace \u2014 one long shared trajectory prefix,\nseven sub-agent branches \u2014 pinning each request with `X-data-parallel-rank` so\nrouting was the only variable:\n\n| routing key | prefix cache hit rate | wall | mean TTFT |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| per-branch (what we do today) | 9.19% | 768s | 83.0s |\n| per-trajectory | **64.90%** | 406s | 43.0s |\n| single shared cache | 64.90% | 956s | 105.0s |\n\nCo-locating a trajectory's branches recovers everything a single shared cache\nwould give for this shape, which says the partitioning itself is fine and the\nrouting key is what hurts.\n\nPlease read those absolute numbers as a mechanism check, not a prediction of the\nproduction delta: the synthetic deliberately contains no within-branch multi-turn\nreuse, which is where most real hits come from and which already works today.\n\n## The change\n\n`cache_aware` is vllm-router's own default. It keeps a radix tree of prompt\nprefixes, routes to the rank holding the longest match, and falls back to load\nbalancing once a rank is `--balance-abs-threshold` (64) requests ahead. It keys\non prompt content, so it co-locates sub-agent branches without any session\nheader, and it also captures prefixes shared *across* trajectories (system\nprompt, tool definitions, common repo context) that no session-keyed policy can\ncatch. `AIPERF_HTTP_X_SESSION_ID_FROM_CORRELATION_ID` becomes unused and is\ndropped.\n\n## Open questions for review\n\n1. **Validation.** I have not yet run the full `aiperf` replay under\n   `cache_aware`. Doing that here needs `semianalysisai/cc-traces-weka-062126`,\n   which is not in the local HF cache. Happy to drive it through CI instead if\n   that is easier.\n2. **Load balance.** `cache_aware` trades balance for locality. With ISL p95 at\n   373k tokens and only 5.97x max concurrency per rank, the default\n   `cache_threshold 0.3` / `balance_abs_threshold 64` may need tuning. Worth a\n   sweep?\n3. **Scope.** `dsv4_fp4_b200_vllm_mtp.sh` and `dsv4_fp4_b300_vllm_mtp.sh` carry\n   the identical `consistent_hash` block. I left them alone until this is\n   validated on MI355X \u2014 say the word and I will include them.\n\n## Unrelated finding, not fixed here\n\n`VLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL=32768` (set just below this block) is a\nno-op. The CI log shows `Unknown vLLM environment variable detected:\nVLLM_PREFIX_CACHE_RETENTION_INTERVAL`, and the run's own\n`vllm:cache_config_info` reports `prefix_cache_retention_interval 0`. The name\nalso does not exist in current vLLM nightly (`0.3.1.dev251+g0961bbae2`). E4M3 covering\nthe full 512-wide K (rope lanes quantized, no BF16 rope segment) plus a 16B\nfooter of 16 UE8M0 scales over 32-wide groups (the\ndeepseek-ai/FlashMLA#221\nlayout, SM100-only there). Add ModelType::DSV4_1 on top of the ScaleSpec\ngroundwork: GLM53_NOPE-style geometry (D_ROPE=0) composed with a 32-wide\nUE8M0 footer.\n\nKernel side the format is simpler than DSV4 (one 512B bulk per row, a single\nunified block-scaled FP8 QK pass, no rope MMA paths). The two new mechanics:\n\n- the 16B footer row generalizes the scale gather from one uint64_t to a\n  width-selected load (uint4) in both the prefill IO helper and the decode\n  kernel's staged gather;\n- the 32-wide groups constrain the XV W-fold (one scale group per W buffer),\n  so an 8-warp XV split would floor NT_PER_WARP_XV to 0: decode runs a\n  4-math-warp tile at BI=64 (the DOTS3_SWA halving precedent) and prefill is\n  SG-only on the BI=32 producer/consumer tile. The ComputeTraits/SmemLayout\n  aliases now take the XV warp count so the NT_PER_WARP_XV assert evaluates at\n  the warp count the XV MMA actually runs at.\n\nSelection is explicit everywhere (d_qk=512 collides with DSV4, the 528B\npayload with GLM53_NOPE): the functional API gains kv_scale_format=\n\"ue8m0_g32\", the TRTLLM-compat entry kv_cache_format=\"fp8_dsv41\", and the\ndecode-dsv4 FFI takes an explicit model_type (-1 keeps the legacy width\ninference, matching the paged-entry kAuto convention). Dual-cache decode is\nsupported like DSV4; dual-cache prefill (MG_DUAL) is intentionally not\ninstantiated.
